title: Warning Symptoms Are Associated With Survival From Sudden Cardiac Arrest
authors: Marijon E, Uy-Evanado A, Dumas F, Karam N, Reinier K, Teodorescu C, Narayanan K, Gunson K, Jui J, Jouven X, Chugh SS
population: Residents aged 35 to 65 years with sudden cardiac arrest in the northwestern United States, 2002 to 2012 (general population, not athletes)
findings: Of 839 patients with sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) and a comprehensive symptom assessment (mean age 52.6 years, 75% men), 430 (51%) had warning symptoms in the 4 weeks before SCA, mainly chest pain and dyspnea (abstract).
In 93% of symptomatic patients the symptoms recurred within the 24 hours before SCA (abstract).

Only 81 patients (19%) called emergency medical services to report symptoms; survival was 32.1% (95% CI 21.8 to 42.4) when 911 was called against 6.0% (95% CI 3.5 to 8.5) when it was not (P < 0.001) (abstract).
The authors conclude that warning symptoms frequently occur before SCA but most are ignored, and that emergent medical care was associated with survival in patients with symptoms (abstract).
limitations: General-population cohort aged 35 to 65, not runners or exercise-related arrests; recall and response bias; symptom assessment missing for 24% of patients. The abstract names chest pain and dyspnea only.
implications: Supports listing chest pain and unusual breathlessness as signs to stop and call emergency services rather than run on; the engine quotes no survival figure to the runner.
